title: Arrays
summary: Store lists in a column, search them, and turn them into rows and back.
intro: Sometimes a row needs a short list: the tags on a post, the ingredients in a recipe. PostgreSQL can store that list in one column as an array, read items by position, search inside it, and turn it into rows when you need to group or count.
setup:
CREATE TABLE posts (
    id integer,
    title text,
    tags text[]
);
INSERT INTO posts (id, title, tags) VALUES
    (1, 'Intro to SQL', ARRAY['sql', 'beginner']),
    (2, 'Postgres arrays', ARRAY['sql', 'postgres', 'arrays']),
    (3, 'Faster indexes', ARRAY['postgres', 'performance']),
    (4, 'Python for data', ARRAY['python', 'data']),
    (5, 'Joins explained', ARRAY['sql', 'beginner', 'joins']),
    (6, 'Tuning queries', ARRAY['sql', 'postgres', 'performance']);
CREATE TABLE recipes (
    id integer,
    name text,
    ingredients text[]
);
INSERT INTO recipes (id, name, ingredients) VALUES
    (1, 'Pancakes', '{flour,egg,milk,sugar}'),
    (2, 'Omelette', '{egg,milk,cheese}'),
    (3, 'Shortbread', '{flour,butter,sugar}'),
    (4, 'Tomato soup', '{tomato,onion,garlic}'),
    (5, 'Garlic bread', '{bread,butter,garlic}');

steps.title: Array values
steps.body:
An array holds a list of values of one type in a single column. Add `[]` to a type to get its array type: `text[]`, `integer[]`. This lesson uses two tables:

```sql harness
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS posts CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS recipes CASCADE;
{{code}}
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (id integer, title text, tags text[]);
-- (1, 'Intro to SQL', {sql,beginner}) ... 6 posts
CREATE TABLE recipes (id integer, name text, ingredients text[]);
-- (1, 'Pancakes', {flour,egg,milk,sugar}) ... 5 recipes
```

Write an array as `ARRAY['sql', 'beginner']` or as the text literal `'{sql,beginner}'`. The literal is plain text until PostgreSQL knows its type, so in a bare `SELECT` cast it: `'{1,2,3}'::integer[]`. psql prints arrays in braces and quotes items with spaces: `{"olive oil",salt}`.

- `tags[1]` is the first item. Indexes start at 1, and an index past the end gives NULL, not an error.
- `tags[1:2]` is a slice, a new array of items 1 through 2. A slice past the end is shorter or empty.
- `cardinality(tags)` counts the items. An empty array `'{}'` has 0.
- `array_append(tags, 'new')` adds one item at the end. `tags || ARRAY['a', 'b']` joins two arrays.

Watch out: `tags || 'new'` fails with `ERROR:  malformed array literal: "new"`, because PostgreSQL reads the quoted text as an array literal. Use `array_append` or `ARRAY['new']` instead.

These return new arrays. The table stays the same.

example.title: Post tag summary
example.prompt: Print each post's title, its first tag, how many tags it has, and its tags with 'blog' added at the end.
example.code:
SELECT title,
    tags[1] AS first_tag,
    cardinality(tags) AS tag_count,
    array_append(tags, 'blog') AS more_tags
FROM posts
ORDER BY id;
example.explanation: `tags[1]` reads position 1, the first tag. `cardinality(tags)` counts every item in the array. `array_append(tags, 'blog')` returns a copy of the array with one more item, so the stored tags stay the same.

practice.title: Recipe ingredient summary
practice.prompt:
Print a short summary of every recipe's ingredient list.

1. Select the recipe `name`.
2. Select the first two ingredients, as a slice, as `first_two`.
3. Select how many ingredients the recipe has as `ingredient_count`.
4. Select the ingredients with `ARRAY['salt']` joined on the end using `||`, as `with_salt`.
5. Sort by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
     name     |   first_two    | ingredient_count |          with_salt
--------------+----------------+------------------+-----------------------------
 Pancakes     | {flour,egg}    |                4 | {flour,egg,milk,sugar,salt}
 Omelette     | {egg,milk}     |                3 | {egg,milk,cheese,salt}
 Shortbread   | {flour,butter} |                3 | {flour,butter,sugar,salt}
 Tomato soup  | {tomato,onion} |                3 | {tomato,onion,garlic,salt}
 Garlic bread | {bread,butter} |                3 | {bread,butter,garlic,salt}
(5 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: add first_two, ingredient_count, and with_salt
SELECT name
FROM recipes
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT name,
    ingredients[1:2] AS first_two,
    cardinality(ingredients) AS ingredient_count,
    ingredients || ARRAY['salt'] AS with_salt
FROM recipes
ORDER BY id;
hints: A slice puts the first and last position in the brackets with a colon between them.
`||` needs an array on both sides, so build the right side with `ARRAY[...]`.

steps.title: Searching arrays
steps.body:
Three conditions cover most searches in an array column. Each one is a condition, so it goes in `WHERE`.

- `'sql' = ANY(tags)` is true when any item equals `'sql'`. The single value goes on the left.
- `tags @> ARRAY['sql', 'postgres']` means *contains*: every item on the right is somewhere in `tags`, in any order.
- `tags && ARRAY['python', 'data']` means *overlaps*: the arrays share at least one item.

```sql
SELECT ARRAY['a', 'b', 'c'] @> ARRAY['c', 'a'];  -- t
SELECT ARRAY['a', 'b'] && ARRAY['x', 'b'];        -- t
```

So `@>` works like AND across the items you list, and `&&` works like OR. `<@` is the same test as `@>` turned around: `ARRAY['sql'] <@ tags`.

Some gotchas. `@>` and `&&` need both sides to be arrays of the same type, so write `ARRAY['sql']`, not `'sql'`. And a NULL array gives NULL for all three, so `WHERE` drops that row. Plain `=` is different: `ARRAY['a', 'b'] = ARRAY['b', 'a']` is false, because it compares the items in order.

example.title: Find posts by tag
example.prompt: List the posts tagged sql, then the posts tagged both sql and postgres, then the posts tagged python or performance.
example.code:
SELECT id, title
FROM posts
WHERE 'sql' = ANY(tags)
ORDER BY id;

SELECT id, title
FROM posts
WHERE tags @> ARRAY['sql', 'postgres']
ORDER BY id;

SELECT id, title
FROM posts
WHERE tags && ARRAY['python', 'performance']
ORDER BY id;
example.output:
id |      title
----+-----------------
  1 | Intro to SQL
  2 | Postgres arrays
  5 | Joins explained
  6 | Tuning queries
(4 rows)

 id |      title
----+-----------------
  2 | Postgres arrays
  6 | Tuning queries
(2 rows)

 id |      title
----+-----------------
  3 | Faster indexes
  4 | Python for data
  6 | Tuning queries
(3 rows)
example.explanation: `= ANY` checks one tag against each item of the array. `@>` keeps posts whose tags include both `sql` and `postgres`, so `Intro to SQL` is left out. `&&` keeps posts that share at least one tag with the list on the right.

steps.title: Arrays to rows and back
steps.body:
`unnest(array)` turns an array into rows, one per item. It returns rows, so it goes in `FROM`:

```sql
SELECT tag FROM unnest(ARRAY['sql', 'joins']) AS tag;  -- 2 rows
```

To unnest a column, join each row to its own items. `CROSS JOIN unnest(tags) AS tag` pairs every post with each of its tags, so a post with 3 tags becomes 3 rows that keep `title` and `id`. Now `GROUP BY tag` counts posts per tag, like any column. A row whose array is empty or NULL makes no rows at all, so it drops out.

`array_agg(value ORDER BY ...)` goes the other way: it collects a group's values into one array. Without `ORDER BY` inside, the item order is not guaranteed.

`array_to_string(array, ', ')` joins the items into text with a separator and skips NULL items. It works on any array, like a stored column: `array_to_string(tags, ' / ')`. On an aggregate, `array_to_string(array_agg(x ORDER BY x), ', ')` gives the same text as `string_agg(x, ', ' ORDER BY x)`.

example.title: Posts per tag
example.prompt: Count how many posts use each tag, most used first, then list each tag with an array of its post titles.
example.code:
SELECT tag, count(*) AS post_count
FROM posts
CROSS JOIN unnest(tags) AS tag
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY post_count DESC, tag;

SELECT tag, array_agg(title ORDER BY title) AS titles
FROM posts
CROSS JOIN unnest(tags) AS tag
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY tag;
example.explanation: `CROSS JOIN unnest(tags)` makes one row per post and tag, so grouping by `tag` counts posts. Ties in `post_count` are broken by `tag`. In the second query `array_agg` collects the titles of each group in alphabetical order. Titles with spaces print in double quotes because that is how psql shows array items.

practice.title: Recipes per ingredient
practice.prompt:
List every ingredient with the recipes that use it as one line of text.

1. Turn each recipe's ingredients into rows with `CROSS JOIN unnest(ingredients) AS ingredient`.
2. Group by `ingredient` and select it.
3. Collect the recipe names in alphabetical order with `array_agg`, and join them with `', '` using `array_to_string`, as `recipes`.
4. Sort by `ingredient`.

Expected output:

```text
 ingredient |          recipes
------------+---------------------------
 bread      | Garlic bread
 butter     | Garlic bread, Shortbread
 cheese     | Omelette
 egg        | Omelette, Pancakes
 flour      | Pancakes, Shortbread
 garlic     | Garlic bread, Tomato soup
 milk       | Omelette, Pancakes
 onion      | Tomato soup
 sugar      | Pancakes, Shortbread
 tomato     | Tomato soup
(10 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: one row per ingredient with its recipe names as text
SELECT name, ingredients
FROM recipes
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT ingredient,
    array_to_string(array_agg(name ORDER BY name), ', ') AS recipes
FROM recipes
CROSS JOIN unnest(ingredients) AS ingredient
GROUP BY ingredient
ORDER BY ingredient;

recap:
- Write arrays as `ARRAY['a', 'b']` or `'{a,b}'`, in `text[]` or `integer[]` columns.
- `tags[1]` is the first item, `tags[1:2]` a slice, and `cardinality(tags)` the count.
- `array_append(tags, x)` and `||` add items.
- `x = ANY(tags)` tests one value, `@>` means contains all, and `&&` means shares any.
- `CROSS JOIN unnest(tags) AS tag` makes one row per item, and `array_agg(x ORDER BY x)` collects rows back into an array.
- `array_to_string(array, ', ')` turns an array into text.
